hints: Look at the height of the peaks against the horizontal dashed lines as time increases.
Compare the horizontal length of the first full oscillation with the later oscillations on the time axis.
Recall that $f = 1/T$ for a wave, so a shorter time for one oscillation means a larger number of oscillations per second.
walkthrough: Identify the axes: vertical is displacement of one layer of air, horizontal is time. Peak height shows amplitude and horizontal repeat length shows period $T$.
Check amplitude: all positive peaks reach the same upper dashed line and all negative peaks reach the same lower dashed line, so maximum displacement $x_0$ is unchanged.
Check period: the first oscillation takes a longer time to return to the same point in the cycle than the later oscillations, so $T$ is getting smaller.
Use $f = 1/T$. A decreasing $T$ gives an increasing $f$, which matches the cycles crowding together in time.
Wavelength $\lambda$ needs distance information or wave speed $v = f\lambda$ and cannot be found from a displacement-time graph alone. This is option B.

options.A: Amplitude is the maximum displacement. The peaks still just touch the same dashed lines, so amplitude is constant.
options.B: More oscillations fit into the same time interval later in the graph, so the number of oscillations per second is increasing.
options.C: Period is the time for one oscillation on the time axis. That time gets shorter from left to right, so period is decreasing.
options.D: Wavelength is a distance measured on a displacement-distance graph, not on this displacement-time graph, and cannot be read directly here.
